query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: The retention of a single-phase solid-solution structure in near‐equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles under high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric service conditions is governed by lattice distortion–induced sluggish diffusion. In other words, the high mixing entropy creates significant lattice strain that increases atomic diffusion barriers, thereby inhibiting phase separation and elemental segregation.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles (i.e., high‐entropy alloy nanoparticles) with a uniform distribution of constituent elements and a single-phase structure.
generation.intervention: Synthesize two sets of nanoparticles: one set with a near‐equiatomic composition to maximize lattice distortion (high entropy) and a second set with a deliberately non‐equiatomic composition (lower mixing entropy) to reduce lattice distortion, while keeping all other synthesis parameters identical.
generation.conditions: Expose both sets to controlled thermal annealing in environments relevant to catalysis (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric applications (473–1923 K) under inert atmospheres.
generation.structural_mediator: Lattice distortion induced by nearly equal mixing of different elements, which raises diffusion barriers and reduces atomic mobility.
generation.mechanism: The high configurational entropy present in near‐equiatomic systems leads to substantial lattice strain and distortion. This, in turn, increases the activation energy for atomic diffusion (i.e., produces sluggish kinetics) and prevents rapid elemental migration, phase separation, or the formation of intermetallic segregations during high-temperature exposures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical high-temperature treatments, the near‐equiatomic (high entropy) nanoparticles will preserve their uniform, single-phase structure with minimal elemental segregation owing to sluggish diffusion, while the non‐equiatomic nanoparticles will exhibit increased atomic mobility, detectable phase separation, or elemental segregation.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles synthesized with near‐equiatomic composition (high entropy), which have already been confirmed to display uniform elemental distribution and phase stability in initial structural characterizations.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable for nanoparticles with sizes in the nanometer range (e.g., <100 nm) and under service conditions with temperatures from 473 K up to 1923 K. It assumes that no additional external factors (e.g., support interactions or extreme synthesis variations) significantly dominate the diffusion behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative differences in diffusion rates and defect kinetics between equiatomic and non‐equiatomic particles are not currently well established, and potential effects from substrate interactions or synthesis method nuances may introduce variability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of nanoparticles: one with near‐equiatomic (high entropy) composition and a second with off‐equiatomic (lower entropy) composition. Subject both groups to identical annealing cycles across the catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) temperature ranges. Monitor the evolution of the crystal structure and elemental distribution in situ by using techniques such as high-resolution TEM, synchrotron XRD, and elemental mapping.
measurements: Elemental spatial distribution and compositional uniformity
Indicators of phase separation (e.g., appearance of secondary phases)
Atomic diffusion rates estimated via tracer studies or simulation comparisons
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the non‐equiatomic nanoparticles (with reduced lattice distortion) show comparable structural and chemical stability to the near‐equiatomic nanoparticles—meaning no significant difference in phase homogeneity or elemental segregation is observed after identical thermal treatments—then the hypothesis that high mixing entropy and resultant lattice distortion are the dominant factors in stabilizing the nanoparticles is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As described above, during laser irradiation, the conversion of the HEA NPs from the mixed metal precursors adsorbed on LIG involves several processes, including thermal decomposition, metal ion reduction, metallic element melting, molten bead fusion, and fission, depending on the temperature experience. The laser synthesis in this work is based on solid-phase, which is different from liquid-phase synthesis. As the mixed metal precursor is adsorbed on the 3D porous LIG structure and dried before laser irradiation, the size of the nanoparticles can be well controlled by the laser fluence, and the concentration of the precursor due to the limited mobility of the reduced metal species and subsequently the nanoparticles.

The dispersion stability of the MEA-NPs can be explained by the following two reasons. First, we used high temperatures for the MEA-NP synthesis, and as a result, they naturally have high thermal stability. Second, the defects of the carbon nanofibers help to anchor these MEA-NPs onto the substrate with improved thermal stability. In terms of the observed structural stability, we believe that it originates from the entropy stabilization effect. Thermodynamically, multi-elemental mixing increases the mixing of entropy and favors an alloy structure. Kinetically, the mixing among different elements also leads to increased lattice distortion (table S3 for Ru MEA-NPs) and, therefore, sluggish diffusion, which prevents phase separation and elemental segregation (, ). To further verify the structural stability, we performed MD simulations to calculate the self-diffusion coefficient of the Ru element in Ru-5 MEA and compared it with Ru in a binary Ru-Ni alloy. We also simulated the overall diffusion in the MEA-NP using a hybrid MC + MD simulation approach, in which the MC swaps were attempted at a constant frequency during the MD simulation to model the annealing conditions at 773 K. The entropy-stabilized structure has less atom diffusion due to high diffusion barriers and sluggish kinetics, resulting in uniform elemental distribution after annealing. Figure 4D shows the statistical probability of the nearest composition distributions for each element in Ru-5 MEA-NPs, displaying its microscopic/atomic arrangement of different elements. We found the nearest-neighbor sites of each element equal to its nominal composition with only short-range fluctuations. As a comparison, when it is fully diffusion equilibrated, clear elemental segregation, especially for Ru, Rh, and Ni, is observed (fig. S5A), indicating that the entropy-induced slow kinetics are the key to stabilize the structure for thermal annealing. Similar entropy-stabilization results were also found when there is an extension of MC + MD’s time scale to 50 ns (fig. S5B) and in the Ru-4 MEA-NPs (fig. S5, C and D).
